entities.name: Transformers and large language models
entities.criterion: A passage names the family when it names the Transformer architecture (a sequence model built on attention without recurrence) or the class of language models built on it; it describes the family when it states what that architecture or class consists of.

search.venues: arXiv (v1 PDFs and abstract pages of the papers listed), the ACL Anthology (proceedings PDFs), cdn.openai.com (GPT-1 and GPT-2 PDFs).
search.years: 2014-2023 for the texts read; the naming search for "Transformer" in this sense covered only the texts below and their reference lists.
search.methods: Full-text search of the retrieved texts (tools.mjs grep) for "Transformer", "attention" and "large language model"; citation following from GPT-1, GPT-2, GPT-3, BERT and Zhao et al. back to Vaswani et al. and Bahdanau et al.
search.gaps: No index search for "Transformer" as an architecture name before 2017-06 (the word is common in other senses, e.g. electrical transformers and Chomskyan transformations); earlier attention-based models other than Bahdanau et al. were not read. The large-language-model naming records are kept in the term section (th-term-large-language-model), not here.
search.failures: openai.com (GPT-2, GPT-3 and ChatGPT announcement pages) refused with HTTP 403.

entities.note: Large-language-model naming records belong to th-term-large-language-model; foundation-model records to th-term-foundation-model.

entities.name: 'large language model'
entities.criterion: The phrase "large language model(s)" names a language model (a probability model over word sequences, statistical or neural) that the passage distinguishes by its scale of training data or parameters; uses of "large" for vocabulary size, corpus size alone or the model of a large language class are other senses.

search.venues: ACL Anthology (full bibliography with abstracts, anthology+abstracts.bib.gz, retrieved 2026-10-29: 138,796 entries, 21,003 dated 2007 or earlier, of which 2,178 carry abstracts); Crossref (query.bibliographic, publication date to 2006-12-31, first 50 results); arXiv API (abstract phrase search, submitted 1991-01-01 to 2007-12-31, singular and plural). After the audit: the ISCA Archive (ICSLP 96 found through Semantic Scholar’s abstract search); other speech venues (Eurospeech, ICASSP) were not searched systematically.
search.years: To 2007 for the earliest-located search; 2008-2019 in the ACL Anthology bibliography for later uses.
search.methods: Phrase search "large language model(s)" in titles and abstracts (ACL Anthology bibliography, Crossref, arXiv API); full-text search of the retrieved papers; citation following from Brants et al. 2007 (which cites Emami et al. 2007, "Large-scale distributed language modeling", ICASSP, not retrieved).
search.gaps: Title and abstract search only: most pre-2008 ACL entries have no abstract, and full texts were not searched; speech-recognition venues (ICASSP, Interspeech, ICSLP) outside Crossref titles were not searched; Google Scholar and Google Books were not used; non-English expressions were not searched. Crossref returned only "large vocabulary" and "large-scale" titles, none with the phrase.
search.failures: Semantic Scholar search API returned HTTP 429 twice (2026-10-29); no result from it is used.

corrections.reason: The same-family audit found Hu, Turin and Brown (ICSLP 96, October 1996) through a Semantic Scholar abstract search; the draft’s search had not covered the ISCA Archive of speech conferences.

entities.note: The earliest located use is in the statistical (n-gram) sense; the earliest located neural-sense use found by this search is Witteveen and Andrews (2019). See the open question on whether the criterion should require the neural sense.

entities.name: 'foundation model'
entities.criterion: The phrase "foundation model(s)" names a machine-learning model trained on broad data and adapted to many downstream tasks; engineering uses (an elastic or soil foundation model) and "foundational model" are other senses.

search.venues: arXiv API (abstract phrase search "foundation model" and "foundation models", submitted 1991-01-01 to 2021-08-15: 24 results each); ACL Anthology bibliography with abstracts (all entries dated 2021 or earlier).
search.years: To 2021-08-15 (the day before the Bommasani et al. v1 submission).
search.methods: Phrase search in abstracts; for each machine-learning hit, the v1 (and any pre-August-2021 version) PDF was retrieved and searched for the phrase, because the arXiv API searches the latest version.
search.gaps: Abstracts only, except for the version checks; full texts of arXiv papers, journals and conference proceedings outside the ACL Anthology were not searched; Google Scholar not used. The ML-sense hits found (arXiv 2010.03688 AxFormer, 2102.12037 conditional VAEs, 1810.13306 AutoML survey, 2101.09858 facial affect review) carry the phrase only in versions revised in 2022 or later: their v1 texts (and 1810.13306v4, 2102.12037v2) do not contain it. No ACL Anthology title or abstract to 2021 contains the phrase.

claims.subject: th-brants-2007
claims.statement: Brants, Popat, Xu, Och and Dean (2007) use "large language models" for n-gram language models trained on up to two trillion tokens.
claims.qualification: Use. Held the earliest-located role in the draft; displaced on 2026-10-29 by Hu, Turin and Brown (1996). The sense is statistical: n-gram models with up to 300 billion n-grams, not neural networks. The paper uses the phrase as its title and in its conclusion; it does not define it.

evidence.passage: Large Language Models in Machine Translation
We focus on n-gram language models, which are trained on unlabeled monolingual text.
This finding underscores the value of being able to train and apply very large language models

claims.subject: th-witteveen-2019
claims.statement: Witteveen and Andrews (2019) use "large language models" for neural language models such as GPT-2.
claims.qualification: The earliest located use in the neural sense by the ACL Anthology title and abstract search for 2008-2019; other 2019 Anthology abstracts (P19-1598, D19-1625) also use the phrase. Not evidence of coinage of the neural sense.

evidence.passage: Paraphrasing with Large Language Models
Recently, large language models such as GPT2 have shown themselves to be extremely adept at text generation

claims.subject: kp-language-models-few-shot-learners-2020
claims.statement: The GPT-3 paper (arXiv v1, 2020) uses "a large language model" of the model in work it cites as [RRS20].
claims.qualification: A use in passing; the paper calls GPT-3 itself "an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters".

evidence.passage: [RRS20] recently demonstrated that a large language model can perform surprisingly well directly answering the questions without conditioning on auxilliary information.

claims.subject: kp-gpt-4-technical-report-2023
claims.statement: The GPT-4 Technical Report (arXiv v1, 2023) compares GPT-4 with "previous large language models".
claims.qualification: A use; the report calls GPT-4 "a large-scale, multimodal model" and does not define the phrase.

evidence.passage: On a suite of traditional NLP benchmarks, GPT-4 outperforms both previous large language models and most state-of-the-art systems

claims.subject: th-zhao-2023-llm-survey
claims.statement: Zhao et al. (arXiv v1, 2023) define large language models as Transformer-based language models with hundreds of billions or more parameters trained on massive text data.
claims.qualification: The survey's working definition; its conclusion narrows its scope to models larger than 10B parameters, and p. 1 speaks of "tens or hundreds of billions". Other texts use the phrase without this threshold.

evidence.passage: Typically, large language models (LLMs) refer to language models that contain hundreds of billions (or more) of parameters
Specifically, LLMs are built upon the Transformer architecture
We focus on the discussion of large-sized models (i.e., having a size larger than 10B)

claims.subject: th-zhao-2023-llm-survey
claims.statement: Zhao et al. (arXiv v1, 2023) state that the research community uses "large language models (LLM)" for pre-trained language models of significant size.
claims.qualification: A use, and the survey's own account of the term's scope. Its words "has coined the term" are the survey's statement and are recorded as attributed statements (th-term-llm-zhao-credits-*), not as a dating of the term; the survey does not mention Brants et al. 2007.

evidence.passage: the research community has coined the term large language models (LLM) for the PLMs of significant size (e.g., containing tens or hundreds of billions of parameters)

claims.subject: th-zhao-2023-llm-survey
claims.statement: According to Zhao et al. (2023), the term "large language models (LLM)" for large-sized pre-trained language models is a coinage of the research community, for which the survey cites the Chinchilla paper among four works.
claims.qualification: The survey's attributed statement, not the pack's: it credits "the research community" and cites [32-35] as examples; it does not say that the Chinchilla paper named the term. It conflicts in date with the earliest located use (Brants et al. 2007, statistical sense); the pack does not resolve it.

credit.contribution: use of the term "large language models (LLM)" for large-sized pre-trained language models
credit.attribution: According to Zhao et al. (2023), citing [32-35]

evidence.passage: Thus, the research community coins the term “large language models (LLM)” … for these large-sized PLMs [32–35].

evidence.locator: PDF p. 3, section 2 and PDF p. 34, references
evidence.passage: Reference [34] is the work discussed on p. 3 as the study of "the optimal schedule" among model size, data size and compute; in the reference list it is Hoffmann et al., "Training compute-optimal large language models", abs/2203.15556, 2022.
evidence.note: The reference numbers are separated from their entries in the text layer; [34] is identified by the body text and the order of entries.

claims.subject: th-zhao-2023-llm-survey
claims.statement: According to Zhao et al. (2023), the term "large language models (LLM)" is a coinage of the research community, for which the survey cites the chain-of-thought prompting paper among four works.
claims.qualification: The survey's attributed statement; [33] is identified from the reference order and its use for the CoinFlip task (PDF p. 24). The other two cited works (Shanahan 2022; Taylor et al., Galactica, 2022) have no record in the dataset or the key-papers pack and are not recorded.

credit.contribution: use of the term "large language models (LLM)" for large-sized pre-trained language models
credit.attribution: According to Zhao et al. (2023), citing [32-35]

evidence.passage: Thus, the research community coins the term “large language models (LLM)” … for these large-sized PLMs [32–35].
Reference [33] is Wei et al., "Chain of thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models", abs/2201.11903, 2022.
evidence.note: Identified by the order of entries in the text layer.

claims.subject: kp-opportunities-risks-foundation-models-2021
claims.statement: Bommasani et al. (arXiv v1, 2021) name models trained on broad data at scale and adaptable to many downstream tasks "foundation models".
claims.qualification: Earliest located in the machine-learning sense by the recorded search. The report states that its authors chose to coin the term (th-term-fm-bommasani-2021-naming); that is the text's own statement. Earlier engineering uses are other senses.

evidence.passage: We call these models foundation models to underscore their critically central yet incomplete character.
AI is undergoing a paradigm shift with the rise of models (e.g., BERT, DALL-E, GPT-3) that are trained on broad data at scale and are adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks.
evidence.note: The sentence that “these models” refers to (audit B).

claims.subject: kp-opportunities-risks-foundation-models-2021
claims.statement: Bommasani et al. (2021) define a foundation model as a model trained on broad data at scale that serves as the common basis from which task-specific models are built by adaptation.
claims.qualification: The report's definition; it gives BERT, DALL-E and GPT-3 as examples.

evidence.passage: models (e.g., BERT, DALL-E, GPT-3) that are trained on broad data at scale and are adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks
a foundation model is itself incomplete but serves as the common basis from which many task-specific models are built via adaptation

claims.subject: kp-opportunities-risks-foundation-models-2021

object.value: The report's authors chose the new term "foundation models" after surveying existing terms such as "pretrained model" and "self-supervised model".

claims.statement: Bommasani et al. (2021) state that, having surveyed existing terms such as "pretrained model" and "self-supervised model", they chose to coin the new term "foundation models".
claims.qualification: The text's own priority statement ("coin the new term"), recorded as its statement; the pack does not adopt it. The section heading is "Naming" (1.1.1).

evidence.passage: Existing terms (e.g., pretrained model, self-supervised model) partially capture the technical dimension of these models
Having surveyed existing terms and numerous alternatives, we chose to coin the new term foundation models to identify the models, and the emerging paradigm, that are the subject of this report.

claims.subject: th-lyashenko-2013-contact
claims.statement: Lyashenko, Pastewka and Persson (arXiv, 2013) use "elastic foundation model" for a one-dimensional model in contact mechanics.
claims.qualification: Other sense (engineering mechanics), recorded to show that the phrase predates 2021 in another field; one of several such uses in the arXiv search (Winkler foundation models, soil foundations).

evidence.passage: mapping the problem on an effective one dimensional (1D) elastic foundation model

claims.subject: attention-all-you-need
claims.statement: Vaswani et al. (arXiv v1, 2017) name a network architecture based solely on attention mechanisms "the Transformer".
claims.qualification: Earliest located naming of the architecture by the recorded search, which did not search indexes for earlier uses of "Transformer" in this sense. The conclusion's "the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention" is the text's own priority statement.

evidence.passage: We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
the Transformer, the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention

claims.subject: attention-all-you-need
claims.statement: Vaswani et al. (2017) describe the Transformer as an encoder-decoder model that replaces recurrent layers with multi-headed self-attention.
claims.qualification: The paper's description of its own architecture, not a definition of the later family of large language models.

evidence.passage: replacing the recurrent layers most commonly used in encoder-decoder architectures with multi-headed self-attention

claims.subject: attention-all-you-need
claims.statement: Vaswani et al. (2017) attribute additive attention, one of the two most commonly used attention functions, to Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014).
claims.qualification: A citation for one attention function, kept as the citing text's attribution; it does not state that Bahdanau et al. devised attention in general.

evidence.passage: The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention [2], and dot-product (multiplicative) attention.
Reference [2] is Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio, "Neural machine translation by jointly learning to align and translate", CoRR abs/1409.0473, 2014.

claims.subject: kp-neural-machine-translation-by-jointly-2014
claims.statement: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (arXiv v1, 2014) propose letting a neural translation model (soft-)search for the parts of a source sentence relevant to each target word, instead of a fixed-length vector.
claims.qualification: The v1 abstract does not use the word "attention" in the quoted passage; the link to the Transformer family rests on Vaswani et al.'s citation (th-fam-tllm-attention-credits-bahdanau), not on this text.

evidence.passage: we conjecture that the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck in improving the performance of this basic encoder–decoder architecture, and propose to extend this by allowing a model to automatically (soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word

claims.subject: kp-improving-language-understanding-by-generative-2018
claims.statement: Radford, Narasimhan, Salimans and Sutskever (2018) report using the Transformer, citing Vaswani et al., as their model architecture.

time.note: Year from a later citation (claimed); the PDF is undated.

claims.qualification: The paper reports a multi-layer Transformer decoder for its language model; reference [62] is Vaswani et al.

evidence.passage: For our model architecture, we use the Transformer [62], which has been shown to perform strongly on various tasks such as machine translation [62]
we use a multi-layer Transformer decoder [34] for the language model, which is a variant of the transformer [62]

claims.subject: kp-improving-language-understanding-by-generative-2018
claims.statement: Radford et al. (2018) describe generative pre-training of a language model on unlabeled text followed by discriminative fine-tuning on each task.
claims.qualification: A method statement from the abstract; the paper does not call its model a large language model.

evidence.passage: large gains on these tasks can be realized by generative pre-training of a language model on a diverse corpus of unlabeled text, followed by discriminative fine-tuning on each specific task.

claims.subject: kp-bert-pre-training-deep-bidirectional-2019
claims.statement: Devlin, Chang, Lee and Toutanova (arXiv v1, 2018) report that BERT's architecture is a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder based on Vaswani et al.'s original implementation.
claims.qualification: The paper's statement of its architecture.

evidence.passage: We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.
BERT’s model architecture is a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder based on the original implementation described in Vaswani et al. (2017)

claims.subject: kp-language-models-unsupervised-multitask-learners-2019
claims.statement: Radford et al. (2019) report a Transformer-based architecture, citing Vaswani et al., for the GPT-2 language models.
